sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 52 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God.
study.intro: Nine verses confront a boastful, deceitful man whose words destroyed others, announce that God will uproot him, and contrast him with a person rooted like an olive tree in God's house.
study.context: The heading names David and the occasion: Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, told Saul that David had visited Ahimelech the priest at Nob. 1 Samuel 21:1–9 and 22:6–23 record that Saul then had Doeg kill eighty-five priests and strike the town of Nob. Verses 1–4 address the 'mighty man' whose tongue is a razor; verses 5–7 announce God's judgment and the righteous seeing it; verses 8–9 contrast the speaker, rooted in God's love. The mocking in verse 6 is read as the righteous recognizing God's justice, not as permission to gloat over anyone's ruin (compare Proverbs 24:17). The notes say Doeg was an Edomite because the text does, not as a comment on any people today. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: The heading names David and the occasion when Doeg the Edomite informed on him to Saul. His profile covers his years fleeing Saul, including the visit to Nob. Doeg, Saul and Ahimelech are named in the heading but have no profiles in the app, so they are not linked. Planned paintings show olive trees, razors, tents and landscapes; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Why boast of evil?
verses.heading: Confronting the mighty man
verses.meaning: The heading names David and links the psalm to Doeg the Edomite, who informed Saul that David had been helped by the priest Ahimelech. David asks the 'mighty man' why he boasts of evil. Doeg's report led to a massacre of priests. Yet the verse ends with a contrast: God's loving devotion endures all day long. The boaster's power is temporary; God's love is constant. That contrast shapes the whole psalm.
verses.context: 1 Samuel 21:7 places Doeg at Nob when David arrived, and 1 Samuel 22:9–19 records his report and the killing of the priests. 1 Samuel 22:22 records David's grief, 'I am responsible for the death of all your father's house.'
explore: Mighty man
The title is ironic. Doeg's 'might' was cruelty, not true strength.
Loving devotion endures
God's love outlasts the boaster. It is steady all day long.
verses.reflect: Whose boasting of evil discourages you? How does God's enduring love answer it?
verses.alt: Lamps still burn in a ransacked priestly town at dusk.

verses.title: Tongue like a razor
verses.heading: Words that destroy
verses.meaning: Your tongue devises destruction like a sharpened razor, O worker of deceit. Doeg's weapon was his tongue. A razor cuts quickly and cleanly; his words did the same. He 'devises destruction,' meaning his speech was planned to harm. Though what he reported may have been technically true, his purpose was deceitful and destructive. The verse warns that words can be weapons.
verses.context: Psalm 57:4 speaks of tongues like sharp swords, and James 3:8 calls the tongue a restless evil. Proverbs 12:18 contrasts reckless words with healing words.
explore: Sharpened razor
Words can cut deeply. Doeg's speech was precise and harmful.
Worker of deceit
His purpose was destructive. Truthful-sounding words can deceive.
verses.reflect: How have your words cut someone? How could you use your words to heal instead?
verses.alt: An ancient bronze razor gleams on a dark stone.

verses.title: Love evil more than good
verses.heading: Twisted desires
verses.meaning: You love evil more than good, falsehood more than speaking truth. Selah. The problem goes beyond words to the heart. Doeg loves the wrong things. He prefers evil to good and lies to truth. The choices reveal his desires. Selah pauses the song to let the indictment sink in. The verse shows that sinful speech comes from disordered love.
verses.context: Isaiah 5:20 warns those who call evil good, and John 3:19 says people loved darkness rather than light. Psalm 52:3 diagnoses the root of Doeg's speech.
explore: Love evil
The problem lies in desire. Doeg prefers what is wrong and chooses it gladly.
Selah
The pause invites reflection. The charge is serious.
verses.reflect: What do you love most? Do your desires lead you toward truth or away from it?
verses.alt: A thorny bramble is tended in a pot while a fruit tree withers beside it.

verses.title: Words that devour
verses.heading: A deceitful tongue
verses.meaning: You love every word that devours, O deceitful tongue. David addresses the tongue itself. Doeg loves words that swallow up and destroy. His speech is like an animal that devours. The verse repeats the theme of verses 2–3 with greater intensity. Words are not neutral; they can consume reputations and lives.
verses.context: Proverbs 18:8 says the words of a gossip are like choice morsels, and Galatians 5:15 warns, 'If you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out.' Psalm 52:4 describes words that destroy.
explore: Every word that devours
Doeg relishes destructive speech. He enjoys harming others with words.
Deceitful tongue
David addresses the tongue directly. Speech is the instrument of his evil.
verses.reflect: Do you enjoy words that hurt others? How could you love words that build up instead?
verses.alt: A wildfire races through dry grass toward a village.

verses.title: Uprooted from the land of the living
verses.heading: God's judgment on the boaster
verses.meaning: Surely God will bring you down to everlasting ruin; He will snatch you up and tear you away from your tent; He will uproot you from the land of the living. Selah. God will act. The boaster will be brought down, snatched from his home and uprooted like a plant. The images are of complete removal. This is David's confidence that God will judge evil, not his own plan for vengeance. Selah marks the weight of the warning.
verses.context: Psalm 37:35–36 describes a flourishing wicked man who soon was gone, and Proverbs 2:22 says the wicked will be uprooted. Psalm 52:5 leaves judgment to God.
explore: Everlasting ruin
God's judgment is final. The boaster's power will not last.
Uproot you
The image is a plant torn from the soil. It contrasts with the olive tree of verse 8.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God will judge evil free you from taking revenge?
verses.alt: A large tree lies uprooted after a storm with roots in the air.

verses.title: The righteous will see
verses.heading: Awe at God's justice
verses.meaning: The righteous will see and fear; they will mock the evildoer, saying, the righteous respond to God's judgment with fear and with words recorded in verse 7. The fear is reverent awe at God's justice. The 'mocking' is better understood as sober recognition that the boaster's way failed, not cruel gloating. Proverbs 24:17 warns against rejoicing when an enemy falls. The righteous learn from what they see.
verses.context: Psalm 64:9 says all people will fear and proclaim God's works, and Proverbs 24:17–18 warns, 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls.' The notes read verse 6 as a lesson learned, not as cruelty.
explore: See and fear
The righteous watch God act. They respond with reverence.
Mock the evildoer
The words point out the folly of the boaster. They draw a lesson rather than celebrate pain.
verses.reflect: How do you respond when someone who did wrong faces consequences?
verses.alt: Onlookers stand quietly at the edge of a ruined estate.

verses.title: Did not make God his refuge
verses.heading: The lesson of the boaster's fall
verses.meaning: 'Look at the man who did not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and strengthened himself by destruction.' Here is the lesson. The boaster's error was trusting wealth and destruction instead of God. He made himself strong by harming others. The verse names three things: no refuge in God, trust in riches, strength through destruction. Together they explain his fall.
verses.context: Psalm 49:6 describes those who trust in wealth, and 1 Timothy 6:17 warns the rich not to hope in riches. Psalm 52:7 adds strength gained by harming others.
explore: Did not make God his refuge
His basic failure was not trusting God. Everything else followed.
Strengthened by destruction
He built his power by hurting others. It could not last.
verses.reflect: Where do you find your security? Is it God, or something else?
verses.alt: A collapsed treasure house lies open with coins spilled in rubble.

verses.title: An olive tree flourishing
verses.heading: Rooted in God's love
verses.meaning: But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God; I trust in the loving devotion of God forever and ever. The contrast is complete. The boaster is uprooted; David is like a living olive tree in God's house. Olive trees live for centuries, bear fruit and are evergreen. David's security is God's loving devotion, not wealth. He trusts it forever. The image is one of steady, long-lasting life.
verses.context: Psalm 1:3 pictures the righteous as a tree planted by streams, and Jeremiah 11:16 calls Israel a green olive tree. Psalm 92:12–13 says the righteous flourish in the courts of God.
explore: Olive tree
Olives live for centuries. David's life in God is lasting and fruitful.
Loving devotion forever
David's trust rests on God's love, not on wealth. That love never comes to an end.
verses.reflect: What would it mean for you to be rooted in God's love like an olive tree?
verses.alt: An ancient olive tree flourishes in a temple courtyard.

verses.title: Because You have done it
verses.heading: Praise and waiting
verses.meaning: I will praise You forever, because You have done it. I will wait on Your name, for it is good, in the presence of Your saints. David promises lasting praise because God has acted, perhaps by protecting him or by judging the boaster. He will wait on God's name, meaning he will hope in God's character. He will do this in the company of God's faithful people. Worship is communal and patient.
verses.context: Psalm 27:14 says, 'Wait patiently for the LORD,' and Psalm 22:22 says, 'I will praise You in the assembly.' Psalm 52:9 joins praise, waiting and community.
explore: Because You have done it
God has acted. Praise responds to what He has done.
In the presence of Your saints
David praises among the faithful. Worship is shared.
verses.reflect: What has God done that you could praise Him for today among others?
verses.alt: Worshipers gather under olive trees with lamps at evening.
